newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania blasts Burundi junta over executions.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania blasts Burundi junta over executions.

text.p: Tanzania on Sunday accused Burundi's military junta of trying to sabotage peace efforts by executing six people convicted of involvement in ethnic violence.
The United States and Amnesty International had earlier condemned the executions of the six, three Hutus, two Tutsis and a Twa.
In an unusually strongly-worded statement, Tanzania's foreign ministry accused Burundi's military rulers of trying to sabotage international efforts to bring peace to the ethnically divided nation.

Tanzanian retired president Julius Nyerere, named by regional states to mediate with Burundi on their demand for the restoration of constitutional rule there, announced last week that all-party talks aimed at resolving the Burundi civil war would start on August 25.

"Tanzania has learned with great shock and consternation about the fate of Burundi nationals who were summarily executed on July 31 because they were allegedly found guilty of massacring their fellow citizens following the (1993) assassination of the first democratically elected president of Burundi, Melchior Ndadaye," the statement said.

It said Tanzania strongly believed that fair trials and justice could not be dispensed by a "military government which abrogated the constitution and is itself an embodiment of illegality and unlawful usurpation of power."

"The fact that the summary trial and the consequent executions have taken place only a few days after Mwalimu (Swahili for "teacher") Nyerere's announcement of the date for commencing the process of reconciliation, is deplorable to say the least.
"It signals a calculated effort to sabotage the work of the facilitator, and of the special envoys to the region, to promote a new negotiated political dispensation to the region."

The August 25 talks, to be held in Arusha, northern Tanzania, would be the first between the government of military leader Pierre Buyoya and the main Hutu rebel group, the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
Buyoya who seized power in a coup a year ago, signed a pre- ceasefire agreement with CNDD in April after secret talks in Rome.
In Brussels on Sunday the CNDD said the hangings carried out in Bujumbura's central prison on Thursday violated the Rome agreement and warned it may pull out of peace talks.

The accord called for the creation of an international crime tribunal to judge acts of genocide and other political crimes committed in Burundi, a former Belgian colony. The trials of the six men were carried by the local judicial authorities.
"If Buyoya continues with his policy of violating the accord we will have to reconsider the talks," CNDD's spokesman Jerome Ndiho told Reuters.
Despite the Rome agreement, violence has continued in Burundi, pitting the Tutsi-dominated military against majority Hutu rebels in a war which has left more than 150,000 people dead since 1993.
Tension is already running high between Tanzania and Burundi following the killing last month of three villagers in Kigoma region, northwest Tanzania, by Burundian soldiers.
